entries.title: How a machine digs a tunnel
entries.answer: One way to dig a tunnel is with a round machine that cuts through earth or rock as it advances. Its head breaks the material into small pieces. Belts, pipes or special carts remove the pieces. The fresh tunnel often needs support, so workers or equipment place walls or pipes behind the cutter as it moves. Machines for wet, loose ground can also press against the digging face to keep soil and water from rushing in.
facts: Builders choose different tools for hard rock and for soft wet soil.

questions.text: What moves huge pieces of ground over longer times?
What kind of travel uses large tunnels beneath some cities?
Why might a city need smaller tunnels and pipes for used water?

entries.title: How a suspension bridge hangs from cables
entries.answer: On a suspension bridge, smaller vertical lines hang the roadway from large curved cables. Towers support the high points of those cables. Strong connections in the ground hold the cables at the ends, otherwise the weight of the roadway would pull them inward. The towers carry much of the load down to their foundations. This arrangement lets builders cross a wide area without planting a row of supports in the middle of rivers or shipping lanes.
facts: The cables mainly experience pulling forces rather than being squeezed.

questions.text: How can a curved bridge carry a load without hanging from cables?
How can triangles keep a bridge from bending too much?
What makes the roadway weigh anything in the first place?

entries.title: How a traffic light can detect a waiting car
entries.answer: Some traffic lights follow a schedule, while others can change when a vehicle is waiting. One kind of detector uses wire arranged in a loop under the road. Electricity in the loop produces a magnetic field, and a large metal vehicle above it changes the electrical behavior a little. The detector sends a message to the traffic signal’s controller. A signal can also detect vehicles using a camera or equipment that sends radio waves.
facts: A detector can tell a signal that a car is in a lane without needing to know who is driving.

questions.text: What can electric current do in a loop of wire?
How can a different road design guide traffic without signals?
How can a measurement become a message to a computer?

entries.title: How an arch bridge carries weight
entries.answer: An arch bridge uses a curved shape to carry loads toward the ground at each end. The stones in a traditional arch lean on one another, so the weight mainly squeezes them together. The curve also pushes outward at both ends. Strong supports on those sides have to keep the feet of the arch from spreading. Builders once used this shape to carry roads and water channels over valleys, often placing many arches in a row.
facts: Stone handles squeezing much better than being pulled apart.

questions.text: What ancient water system used rows of arches?
Which bridge supports its road by hanging it from cables?
Why do other bridges use straight bars instead of curved stones?

entries.title: How an elevator goes up and down
entries.answer: Many elevators hang the car from strong ropes or belts over a powered wheel. A counterweight hangs on the opposite side and helps balance the car’s weight. That way the motor does not need to lift the full weight of the car by itself. Guide rails keep the car moving along the same path. The machine can stop the car level with a floor, and modern elevators have brakes and other protective systems.
facts: Some elevators are raised by a hydraulic piston instead of a moving rope and counterweight.

questions.text: How can a piston lift a load from below?
How can a turning wheel guide a lifting rope?
How does a moving staircase carry people continuously between levels?

entries.title: How can a landfill hold rubbish in one place?
entries.answer: A landfill is a planned place where waste is put for long-term disposal. At many modern sites, workers build sections for rubbish and use barriers to help keep liquids from moving into nearby ground. As one area fills, the waste can be covered and later loads can go to another area. People looking after the site can monitor what happens to water and gas. A landfill takes up land because the rubbish stays there.
facts: Rain and other liquids can pick up material from waste as they move through it.

questions.text: Why might waste first change vehicles on its way to a landfill?
Where do some items go if they can be made into new things?
How can some scraps break down into something people use in soil?

entries.title: How can a postcard travel without an envelope?
entries.answer: A postcard is a stiff card that can carry a message through the mail without an envelope around it. One side may have a picture. The other can hold a note and the details the mail service needs to know where to deliver it. A postcard’s message can be seen by someone handling the card. The size and shape matter because pieces of mail have to pass through different kinds of equipment.
facts: Picture postcards and cards sold with postage already printed on them are both part of U.S. postal history.

questions.text: What shows that a piece of mail has paid postage?
How do the last numbers in an address help with routing?
What do machines check while putting mail into groups?

entries.title: How can a road bridge open so a boat can pass?
entries.answer: A low bridge can carry cars across a river but get in the way of a tall boat. Some movable bridges tilt part of the road up so the boat can pass. Others slide, swing aside, or lift a stretch of road straight up. Before the bridge moves, people on the road must wait on either side. The bridge can close after the boat is clear.
facts: A bridge with a roadway that tips up around a turning point is often called a bascule bridge.

questions.text: How can a canal lock move a boat to another water level?
How can a hinge let a door turn while it stays attached?
Why do cables in a cable-stayed bridge run diagonally?

entries.title: How can a small crack in a road turn into a pothole?
entries.answer: A pothole can start where the road surface or the material underneath has become weak. Water can get through a crack and soften the layers beneath the road. In some weather, freezing and thawing can make the damage worse. As traffic passes, pieces of the weakened surface can loosen and break away. A hole can then grow as more tires hit its edges. Crews can fill the hole and may also need to work on its cause.
facts: Potholes can also form in places where water rarely freezes.

questions.text: Where is rain supposed to go after falling on a street?
How does a plow move snow away from the path people use?
How do crews remove loose material before it reaches a drain?

entries.title: How can an old aluminum can help make new metal products?
entries.answer: An aluminum can can become useful metal again after it has been collected and sorted. At a processing plant, old aluminum can be cleaned and melted. The melted metal can then be shaped into a larger piece that a factory can use. A maker may roll material into sheets for cans or use it for another product. An old can need not keep its shape for the metal in it to be useful.
facts: A new can may contain metal from many old objects, mixed together before being made into sheet.

questions.text: How can cans be separated from other material before melting?
How does recycling a glass bottle use heat too?
Why do some shoppers get money back for returning a used container?

entries.title: How can machines sort so many letters by address?
entries.answer: In a mail processing center, machines can send letters with different destinations along different paths. A printed barcode can carry information about where a piece should go. After reading the code, a machine can put that letter with other pieces headed toward the same area. Some mail needs other kinds of handling, such as pieces that do not fit the machines. Later, mail can be grouped for the routes used by local carriers.
facts: A barcode read by sorting equipment can give it destination information without the machine reading each part of a written address on every pass.

questions.text: What area can a ZIP Code help a machine find?
How can marks on a label stand for information?
What does a letter carrier do after mail is sorted?

entries.title: How can natural gas reach a place far from where it was found?
entries.answer: Natural gas can travel inside long pipelines to areas far from its source. Systems serving towns then use other pipes to bring gas closer to the places that use it. The line going to one building can be much smaller than the lines that move gas across a region. Some places use gas for heat or to power equipment. Gas and drinking water move through different networks of pipes.
facts: Long-distance transmission pipelines and smaller local distribution pipes do different parts of the work.

questions.text: How does a different network deliver electricity to buildings?
How can a building count the water that enters it?
What kinds of building work involve pipes?

entries.title: How can old paper turn into new paper?
entries.answer: Paper is made from a mat of tiny fibers pressed together. At a paper mill, old paper can be mixed with water so the fibers separate. The mill can remove things that should not be in the new paper. Then the wet fibers can be spread again, pressed, and dried into a sheet. Some old fibers break into pieces that are too short to keep using, which can limit how many times paper is recycled.
facts: Recycled fibers can be mixed with other fibers to make products that need different strengths.

questions.text: How did paper makers learn to turn plant material into sheets?
How is used paper separated from cans and bottles?
How can recycling a metal can differ from recycling paper?

entries.title: How can people borrow a city bicycle for one trip?
entries.answer: A bike share system makes bicycles available for trips by many different people. In a system with docks, a rider takes a bicycle from a station and can return it to a different station after the trip. Once it is back, someone else can use it. Stations may be placed near parks, neighborhoods, or other kinds of transport. It helps to have a way to see where bicycles and empty docks are available.
facts: Some bike share systems use docks, and others use marked parking areas or a different way to end a trip.

questions.text: How do other points around a city help people make short trips?
What changes when someone shifts gears on a bicycle?
Who plans paths and other outdoor spaces that help people get around?

entries.title: How can rain go down through a paved surface?
entries.answer: Many paved surfaces send water running sideways. A permeable pavement has small holes in its material or narrow open spaces between its pieces. These let some water move down through the surface to the layers below. A layer of loose stone can hold some of that water for a while. Depending on the design, the water can then soak into the soil or be carried away by a drain.
facts: Some parking areas and walking paths use blocks with spaces that let water pass between them.

questions.text: Where does water go when a street sends it to a drain?
How can a low garden give rain a place to collect and soak in?
Why do small spaces between fibers give water a path through a towel?

entries.title: How can used water go uphill inside a sewer?
entries.answer: Many sewers let used water flow downhill through pipes. A route cannot always keep going down, because the treatment plant or the next useful pipe may be higher than the low point the water has reached. A lift station can collect water there and pump it to a higher place. From that point, the water can go downhill again where the pipe allows it. Several parts of the trip may work differently.
facts: A pipe that carries pumped water under pressure is sometimes called a force main.

questions.text: What happens after used water reaches a treatment plant?
Who watches over machines at a water plant?
Why does the pipe below a sink often have a bend?

entries.title: How can you raise a flag by pulling down?
entries.answer: On many flagpoles, a rope travels over a small wheel at the top. The wheel guides the rope as it moves around it. If you pull one side down, the other side goes up and can carry the flag with it. The wheel changes the direction of your pull, so you can stay on the ground to raise something far above your head.
facts: One fixed pulley can change the direction of a pull without making the load much lighter.

questions.text: How do cranes use moving wheels to lift a load?
How does a wheel and axle turn as a pair?
Why is a long wrench handle useful when turning something?

entries.title: How canal locks raise and lower boats
entries.answer: A lock is a short section of water with gates at both ends. A boat enters while the lock’s water matches the level outside the open gate. Once inside, the gate shuts. Water flows in from the higher side or drains to the lower side, and the floating boat moves up or down with it. When the water matches the next part of the canal, the other gate can open and the boat moves on.
facts: A boat keeps floating throughout the change in height.

questions.text: Why can water stand at different heights on two sides of a dam?
What holds a heavy ship up as the lock fills?
How did Roman builders move water without pumping it uphill?

entries.title: How dams hold and release water
entries.answer: A dam is a barrier built across a valley or a river. Water gathers behind it in a reservoir. People can release water when fields or towns need it or send it through turbines to make electricity. During heavy rain, some dams hold back part of a flood for a short time. A spillway lets extra water go around or over the dam safely. Dams can also change where fish travel and where sediment collects.
facts: A reservoir can store water between wet and dry seasons.

questions.text: How does falling water make electricity at some dams?
How can boats get past a place where water stands at different heights?
What happens to bits of rock that flowing water can lift and carry?

entries.title: How did a wire let messages cross the ocean?
entries.answer: A telegraph cable stretched across the Atlantic could carry pulses from one shore to the other. A ship laid the cable along the ocean floor between Ireland and Newfoundland. A covering helped keep seawater away from the wires inside. Before that link, news had to travel across the ocean with a ship. A message on a working cable could arrive while the sender was still near the telegraph key.
facts: A lasting transatlantic telegraph cable began working in 1866 after earlier attempts.

questions.text: How could short and long pulses stand for letters?
How do computers send messages through modern links?
How can ships use sound to learn about the ocean floor?

entries.title: How do shipping containers move from a ship to land?
entries.answer: Large boxes called shipping containers can ride on a ship, railroad car, or truck. At a port, a tall crane can lift a box from the ship, carry it over the dock, and lower it onto a waiting area or vehicle. Since the box stays closed during the move, workers can send many small goods onward together instead of transferring each item separately.
facts: Containers often come in standard sizes so builders can plan how to stack and move them.

questions.text: How does a crane hold and raise a heavy load?
How can tugboats help a container ship get to the dock?
How can a ferry take an entire car instead of one box?

entries.title: How do snowplows make a path along a street?
entries.answer: A snowplow uses a wide blade to push snow out of a travel path. Moving the snow creates a clearer path for the next vehicle, but the snow is still somewhere nearby. A crew might make several passes if the street is wide or more snow keeps falling. When a city has many streets, crews follow plans that can give some routes early attention, such as roads that serve important buildings.
facts: In some cities, trucks carry extra snow away when there is not enough room to keep it beside a street.

questions.text: Why can salt make it harder for some ice to stay frozen?
How can water and cold help damage a road surface?
What different kind of vehicle takes loose dirt off streets?

entries.title: How does a road crossing warn that a train is coming?
entries.answer: At some crossings, a road and railway meet without a bridge between them. A busy crossing may have flashing lights, bells, and gates that move down when a train approaches. The warnings tell people on the road to wait while the train uses the crossing. Some crossings have signs instead of moving gates, so the signs are important even when you do not hear a bell.
facts: The large X-shaped railroad crossing sign is often called a crossbuck in the United States.

questions.text: What do railroad signals tell a train crew?
How does a traffic signal know a car is waiting?
How can a train take one track instead of the one beside it?

entries.title: How does a tracking page know where a package has been?
entries.answer: A package that can be tracked has a number that connects it to a set of records. Machines or workers can scan its label at different stops. The service records things such as arrival at a facility, and those records can show up on the tracking page. The package can spend time traveling between scans. In that case, the most recent update tells you where something was recorded, rather than showing its position moving along a road.
facts: A tracking page can have information before the first trip if the sender has already provided the service with a label record.

questions.text: What happens near the end of a package’s trip?
How can a barcode send a letter down the right path?
Where can goods wait between different trips?

entries.title: How does a water meter know how much water a building used?
entries.answer: A water meter measures the amount of water passing along a pipe. When someone uses a sink or a shower, water can pass through the building’s meter on its way there. The reading keeps a running total. Comparing two readings shows how much water passed in the time between them. A reading from last week and a reading from today can tell a different story from either number alone.
facts: Water meters may show amounts in units such as gallons or cubic feet.

questions.text: How can another meter track energy that enters a building?
Who connects the pipes that bring water to a room?
What can happen to water before it is sent to buildings?

entries.title: How drinking water gets cleaned
entries.answer: Water from a river or lake can carry dirt and tiny living things. A treatment plant can add substances that help tiny bits of dirt clump together. Heavy clumps settle, and the water then goes through filters that catch more particles. Disinfection uses methods such as chlorine or ultraviolet light to kill or inactivate many germs. The exact steps depend on the source and the quality of the water. Pipes carry the cleaned water to buildings.
facts: Very clear water can still contain things too small to see.

questions.text: How does treated water reach taps with enough pressure?
What happens to water after it goes down a sink?
How did water get to a river or lake first?

entries.title: How electricity gets to your home
entries.answer: Power plants and other sources make electricity in many places. The power grid links these sources to towns, cities and buildings. Thick wires carry power a long way, often at high voltage to reduce energy lost along the way. Along that route, transformers lower the voltage for smaller local wires and for use in homes. Grid operators try to match the supply of electricity with what people are using at each moment.
facts: A substation helps put power onto different lines or changes the voltage to serve a local area.

questions.text: What makes the current that can travel through power lines?
How can some buildings make part of their own electricity?
How does a closed path let a lamp use electrical energy?

entries.title: How escalator steps go flat at the top
entries.answer: An escalator runs a loop of steps around on a long chain. The visible steps ride upward or downward on wheels set in tracks. The tracks change their height relative to one another so the steps stay level where you stand but flatten together at the ends. After sliding under the landing, the steps loop around and travel back underneath. A second moving loop gives people a handrail that travels alongside them.
facts: An escalator and a moving walkway both use a returning loop hidden beneath the visible path.

questions.text: How does an elevator move a whole room between floors?
How can the wheels under a loaded step turn smoothly?
What parts can transfer power from a motor to a chain?

entries.title: How railway signals help keep trains apart
entries.answer: One way to manage a railway is to divide it into sections called blocks. Equipment can tell a signaling system whether a train is in a block. Signals then help the next driver or automatic controls know whether the route ahead is available. This matters because a heavy train needs a long distance to stop, so relying only on seeing another train could leave too little time. Railways use several ways to detect trains and share information.
facts: Some signal systems use equipment in the tracks to tell whether a train is present.

questions.text: What physical parts let trains take different paths?
Why is separation important on a city line with frequent trains?
How is separation also important for planes near airports?

entries.title: How trains change tracks without steering
entries.answer: Train wheels follow metal rails, so a driver cannot turn a train the way a driver steers a car. At a junction, two short, tapered rails can move a little sideways. In one position they guide the wheels along the main track. In the other they make a smooth path into the branching track. Signals help manage which trains can use that part of the railway. The track arrangement has to be ready before the first wheels reach it.
facts: The moving parts that guide the wheels are called switch points.

questions.text: Why does a subway system also need track junctions?
How did older trains get the power to turn the wheels that follow the rails?
Why do very fast trains usually run on specially designed tracks?

entries.title: What do the big numbers at the end of a runway mean?
entries.answer: A runway is a strip where an aircraft can take off and land. Large numbers at the ends usually describe the direction a plane faces as it goes along the strip. In the United States, the numbers usually come from the direction measured with a magnetic compass, rounded and shortened. The other end points nearly the opposite way. White lines down the middle can mark the center, and other markings can show where a landing area begins.
facts: At airports with several parallel runways, letters sometimes tell apart strips that have nearly the same direction.

questions.text: Why can a compass and a map show slightly different north directions?
Who helps different planes use the same runways without crossing paths?
What happens to the wings when a plane is getting ready to land?

entries.title: What do the five numbers in a ZIP Code help the mail do?
entries.answer: A ZIP Code is part of a mailing address in the United States. The digits help the Postal Service direct mail toward the right delivery area. Many addresses share the same five digits. Think of a pile of letters going across the country. Postal workers can group them by destination before the letters ever reach the people who deliver them. The street address still tells a carrier where within an area the letter belongs.
facts: A ZIP Code may have four extra digits after a hyphen that help describe a smaller part of a delivery area.

questions.text: How does a sorting machine use address information?
How do postal workers know where a letter came from?
Who carries letters to individual addresses?

entries.title: What does an electricity meter count?
entries.answer: An electricity meter measures how much electrical energy goes into a building. The reading can grow more quickly when many things use electricity at once or when something that uses a lot of power runs. A common unit on a bill is the kilowatt-hour. That is the energy used by one kilowatt of power running for an hour. A meter keeps adding to its count as time passes.
facts: Power describes how fast energy is being used. The meter counts the amount used over time.

questions.text: How can electricity travel from a source to buildings?
How is water use measured in another part of the building?
Who checks the electrical parts inside a building?

entries.title: What happens around an airplane between flights?
entries.answer: After a plane reaches its gate, other workers get it ready for its next trip. Some workers move luggage between the airplane and the equipment that takes it to another part of the airport. A crew can also bring supplies and check that the plane’s space on the ground is clear for the next step. The teams share the area and have to do jobs in a useful order. Bags need to be ready before the airplane leaves.
facts: People working near a parked airplane are often described as a ground crew or ramp crew.

questions.text: Who checks and repairs airplane equipment?
Why does an airport need people to coordinate airplane movement?
Who plans how things move between different parts of a trip?

entries.title: What happens to a mixed bin of recycling after pickup?
entries.answer: A recycling sorting center separates useful materials that arrive together. The work often starts with a moving belt carrying items past machines or workers. Paper, plastic, metals, and glass may need to go in different directions because each can be made into different things. A center may press some sorted material into dense bundles before it travels onward. Different communities collect different materials, so the mix arriving at a center can vary.
facts: Sorting and making a new product are usually separate steps, and they can happen at different sites.

questions.text: What can happen to an aluminum can after it is sorted?
How can usable fiber come out of an old paper box?
What can happen to an old glass bottle after collection?

entries.title: Where can an old computer or phone go after someone stops using it?
entries.answer: A device that still works may be repaired or passed along for someone else to use. A device that is no longer useful can lose its job as a phone or computer while still containing materials worth keeping. Places that handle electronic recycling can take items apart and separate materials such as metals and plastics. These items need different handling from ordinary paper or cans. Some parts can also go through special recycling programs.
facts: A device contains many kinds of material in a small space, which is one reason it is sorted differently from a single aluminum can.

questions.text: How does a place that handles mixed recycling sort other materials?
How can metal become useful again after an object is no longer needed?
Why might a tiny new part need a very exact shape?

entries.title: Where do gutters take rain that lands on a roof?
entries.answer: Rain hitting a roof can run toward its lower edge. A gutter is a channel that catches some of the water there. The gutter guides the flow toward an opening and down a pipe called a downspout. Moving the water away helps keep it from spilling in one place beside the building. Some systems lead to a drain or send water to a safe place on the ground.
facts: A downspout is the pipe that carries water from the roof gutter toward the ground.

questions.text: How can overlapping shingles guide rain toward a roof’s edge?
Where can rain go after it reaches a street?
How can a path let rain go down through its surface?

entries.title: Where does rain on a street go?
entries.answer: After rain falls on a street, much of it cannot soak through the hard surface. Water runs along slopes and gutters to an opening or grate. Some drains send this water through pipes to a pond, stream or river. The rain can carry soil, trash or oil it picked up along the way. Unlike the water that leaves a sink, stormwater in many places goes through different pipes. Some older systems share pipes for both.
facts: Moving rainwater from hard surfaces is called runoff.

questions.text: How can a planted dip slow water on its way toward a drain?
What happens to used water from a building’s sinks?
Where does water go once it reaches a river?

entries.title: Where water goes after it runs down the drain
entries.answer: Water that leaves sinks or toilets can move through sewer pipes to a treatment plant. Screens catch big pieces of trash first. In tanks, some smaller solid pieces settle while other material floats and can be removed. In another stage, tiny living things help break down much of the waste still mixed into the water. Plants may remove more material and disinfect the water before returning it to a river or using it again.
facts: The settled mixture left from treatment is often called sludge.

questions.text: How is making river water safe to drink a separate job?
Where can treated water go once it returns to a river?
Why do rivers need oxygen for plants, animals and microbes?

entries.title: Why airports have traffic control towers
entries.answer: Many airports have tall towers where controllers can look out at the runways and paths between gates. They talk with pilots and help keep aircraft apart while airplanes land, take off or move on the ground. Other controllers watch displays and coordinate flights farther from an airport. Bad weather may mean only a few planes can use a runway at once. In that case, the controllers and the people planning traffic can change when planes arrive.
facts: Keeping aircraft apart is one of the controller’s most important jobs.

questions.text: What signs help identify the place where a plane is meant to land?
How can a plane get ready to fly more slowly near a runway?
How do railways also keep moving vehicles apart?

entries.title: Why are there loose stones under many train tracks?
entries.answer: Many railroad tracks rest on short supports laid across the track, called ties or sleepers. The ties sit in a bed of broken stone called ballast. The stone helps spread the weight of a train and hold the ties in place. Spaces between pieces of stone also give rainwater somewhere to flow. Workers check and reshape the bed so the tracks keep their planned height and angle.
facts: Some tracks use a solid supporting base instead of a bed of loose stone.

questions.text: How do the shapes of the train wheels and the rails work together?
How can moving rails let a train take another track?
What are the gates for where a road crosses a railroad?

entries.title: Why bridge frames are full of triangles
entries.answer: A rectangular frame can lean sideways if its joints are free to turn. Add a diagonal bar, and you split the frame into two triangles. Three sides of fixed lengths hold one triangle shape, so they resist that sideways change. A truss bridge joins many triangles in a frame. When a car drives across it, some bars are squeezed and some are pulled. The bars spread the car’s load to the bridge’s supports.
facts: A truss needs strong joints as well as strong bars.

questions.text: How does another bridge shape carry loads mostly by squeezing?
How do cables and towers carry the load of a long bridge?
Why can where you apply a force matter as much as the force itself?

entries.title: Why build a circle where roads meet?
entries.answer: A modern roundabout sends traffic around a small island so paths join in the same direction. The road bends as it leads toward the center, which helps drivers slow before entering the circle. Drivers can then move off along the road they need. Where an ordinary crossing allows several paths to cut across one another, a roundabout has fewer places where moving vehicles meet at right angles. The island’s shape helps guide cars, buses and trucks along useful paths.
facts: A roundabout is shaped to make drivers travel more slowly where paths join.

questions.text: What other kind of road crossing uses signals that can detect vehicles?
Why are very fast vehicles better separated from roads and other paths?
What lets tires grip a curved road?

entries.title: Why can a longer ramp be easier to go up?
entries.answer: A ramp connects a lower place to a higher one with a sloping surface. If two ramps reach the same height, the longer one can climb more gradually. A person using a wheelchair can often roll up a gentle ramp more easily than a steep one. Some ramps include a flat space where someone can stop or turn before going on to the next section.
facts: Small curb ramps can help people roll between a sidewalk and a street crossing.

questions.text: How does a sloping surface trade a longer route for a smaller push?
What is another way people can move up a level without using stairs?
How do workers make the ground level beside a hillside?

entries.title: Why can an envelope have two addresses on it?
entries.answer: One address shows where a letter is meant to go. A return address tells postal workers where it came from. If a letter cannot be delivered, the return address can help the service send it back. The two addresses usually have different places on a United States envelope so the reader can tell them apart. That matters when people send mail across a country where some street names are used in many towns.
facts: A postal address can include a person’s name, street, city, and ZIP Code.

questions.text: Why do postal workers use a ZIP Code as well as a street address?
How can pieces of mail be separated by destination?
What does the stamp on an envelope tell the Postal Service?

entries.title: Why do crews check bridges that people already use?
entries.answer: A bridge inspector looks at the condition of a bridge after it has been built. Parts that were new when it opened can change over time. Inspectors can look for things such as damaged pieces or changes in the surface and record what they find. Some important parts are underneath rather than next to the road. The records help people decide which work a bridge needs and what later inspections should pay attention to.
facts: A bridge inspection can involve looking at the parts that support the deck as well as the deck itself.

questions.text: Who plans and designs bridge projects?
Why do some bridges have parts that can shift a little?
Where do a beam’s forces change when it carries a load?

entries.title: Why do many streets have a fire hydrant?
entries.answer: A fire hydrant gives firefighters a place to get water from a supply below or beside the street. In many towns it connects to the same network of water mains that sends water toward buildings. Its connections let a crew bring that water into its equipment at an emergency. Hydrants can be spread across the area a water system serves. The shape above the sidewalk is just one visible part of the system.
facts: The pipe called a water main carries water for a number of places, rather than for just one faucet.

entries.title: Why do public buses stop at certain places along a route?
entries.answer: A public bus can follow a route that links neighborhoods and places people want to visit. Instead of stopping everywhere, it has a set of places where riders can usually get on or off. Shared stops help a route serve many people while keeping the trip moving. A schedule can list when a bus is expected to reach particular stops. Actual arrivals can change when traffic or the number of riders changes.
facts: Stops on opposite sides of a street may serve buses going in different directions.

entries.title: Why do roads have both yellow and white lines?
entries.answer: Painted lines on a road help people understand how the space is divided. In the United States, a yellow center marking can show where lanes for opposite directions meet. White lines often divide lanes going the same way. Other marks can show where a road edge is or where a crossing begins. The markings work together with signs and lights to give people clues about a place even before they reach it.
facts: A road can have different kinds of markings close together because they show different parts of the road.

entries.title: Why do some bridge cables fan out from a tower?
entries.answer: On a cable-stayed bridge, strong cables run from the tower to points on the roadway below. The cables pull on the roadway and help hold it up. They also pull on the tower, which carries their forces down to its supports. Look from the side and you might see the cables spread like a fan, with several ends reaching different parts of the roadway.
facts: The angled cables on a cable-stayed bridge are called stays.

entries.title: Why do some bridges have gaps or metal strips across the roadway?
entries.answer: Many materials get a little longer when they warm up and shorter when they cool. On a long bridge, a small change in each part can add up to noticeable movement. Some bridges have a joint between parts of the roadway that can open or close a little. It still gives wheels a way to cross while making room for the moving bridge parts.
facts: A bridge joint may use metal fingers or a flexible seal, depending on its design.

entries.title: Why does a little stamp help a letter travel?
entries.answer: A postage stamp shows that part or all of the cost of sending a piece of mail has been paid. Think of it as a small label showing that the letter has paid for its trip through the mail system. Stamps can also carry pictures, so two that serve the same purpose can look very different. A postal service can show postage in other ways too, such as a paid label on a package.
facts: The first U.S. postage stamps, issued in 1847, showed Benjamin Franklin and George Washington.

entries.title: Why does a truck brush dirt off the street?
entries.answer: Loose leaves, grit, and bits of litter build up on streets. A street sweeper can move along the road gathering some of that material. Brushes on some sweepers pull it toward the part of the machine that collects it. Sweeping can also keep some dirt out of storm drains, where rain would have carried it. Where cars are parked close together, the sweeper may have trouble reaching the edge of the street.
facts: Cleaning along the curb can matter because loose material often collects at the edge of a road.

entries.title: Why does a wall holding back soil need a strong base?
entries.answer: A retaining wall keeps soil on one side higher than the ground on the other side. The soil presses sideways, even though its weight pulls down. The wall has to pass those forces into parts that can hold it in place. A wide base or other supports can help the wall resist sliding or tipping. Different walls carry those pushes in different ways.
facts: A retaining wall can make room for a path beside a hillside.

entries.title: Why might a garbage truck stop before reaching a landfill?
entries.answer: A truck that collects rubbish can fill up long before it reaches the place where that rubbish is handled. A waste transfer station gives collection trucks a nearer place to unload. The station can combine the loads of several trucks onto a larger vehicle for the longer trip. Collection crews can then go back to their routes. Not every place uses a transfer station, and the destination depends on the local system.
facts: The station changes which vehicle carries the load and sends the waste farther along its trip.

entries.title: Why some electrical problems turn the power off
entries.answer: A wire can heat up if more electric current passes through it than it was made to carry. A protective device called a circuit breaker can open the wire’s path automatically. Current then stops flowing along that path, cutting power to the parts it supplies. A fuse serves a similar purpose but uses a small piece of metal that melts to break the path. In either case, opening the circuit helps keep the wiring from overheating.
facts: A circuit breaker and a light switch both open a circuit, but the breaker can do it automatically when there is a problem.

entries.title: Why some gardens are planted lower than the ground
entries.answer: A rain garden looks like a shallow hollow planted with things that can handle occasional wet soil. Water rushing off a roof, road or path can spread out and slow down in the hollow. The slower water has more time to soak through the soil, where some loose bits and other materials can be removed. After the garden drains, the plants can keep growing. Rain gardens can reduce the stream of water reaching a storm drain.
facts: A rain garden holds water for a short time, rather than staying full all year.

entries.title: Why water towers are so tall
entries.answer: A water tower holds a tank high above the ground. Pumps fill the tank when they can, and gravity helps push its stored water down into the town’s pipes. Putting the water higher raises the pressure at a lower tap, much like lifting one end of a hose full of water can make it flow out of the other. The tank can help meet short periods of heavy use, such as when many showers are running together.
facts: A town may use more than one tank where the land has very different heights.
